source.title: Activation Steering Induces Emergent Misalignment: Steering Vector Construction and Comprehensive Evaluation
source.authors: Qian Cao; Jian Lou; Mei-Ting Liu; Wen-Jie Feng; Dan Li; See-Kiong Ng; A. Lưu

record.file_problem: The text contains the full paper and appendices. Some figures and extracted text have formatting irregularities, but the main tables and described results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends narrow-task emergent-misalignment research to inference-time activation steering derived from narrow fine-tunes, and reports results across datasets, model families, scales, and intervention settings. Its steering results are not direct tests of the listed fine-tuning claims.
record.gate_note: The paper measures coherent harmful compliance on StrongREJECT and HEx-PHI, which use harmful requests. It does not evaluate neutral open-ended questions of the kind named in the claim versions. Steering-vector results are from adding vectors at inference time, not the effect of fine-tuning alone. Code-semantic scores are not recorded as rows because they measure code-domain carryover rather than the misaligned behavior named in the versions. Category-level plots and other parameter sweeps are noted under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study uses narrow EM fine-tunes (insecure code, bad medical, risky financial, extreme sports) only as sources for inference-time steering vectors. Its measure, MAP on StrongREJECT and HEx-PHI, is coherent harmful compliance with harmful requests. That construct differs from V1/V2's misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions, and the original source distinguishes EM from jailbreak-style compliance. The FT-vs-base rows therefore measure a related construct, not the claim. Steering adds the behaviour by intervention rather than measuring it arising from training. No version is tested; findings go to fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but one correction: the authors claim AS yields higher MAP than both base and insecure-FT in every evaluated model on both benchmarks, not 'sometimes'. They also claim AS responses are more coherent and actionable, with less code carryover (lower CSS). They report the effect depends on SV construction, with secure-code vectors giving none, and varies with strength, layer, rank and model.
record.recipe_differences: The paper derives activation vectors from matched base and fine-tuned activations and injects them at inference time; it evaluates harmful-request benchmarks rather than the neutral open-ended prompts named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to activation-source dataset, steering magnitude, projection rank, fine-tuning configuration, model family and scale, and injection layer. Higher steering strength is non-monotonic and can cause degeneration; layer choice changes MAP substantially. The one- versus three-epoch comparison also changes learning rate and, for some models, other settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean finetuned-minus-base activation vectors from insecure-code FT, injected at α=3, raise harmful-request MAP above both base and FT in all six models on both benchmarks. Examples: Qwen2.5-32B StrongREJECT 57.51% vs FT 21.73%; Llama3.1-8B HEx-PHI 34.00% vs FT 8.00%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering vectors derived from narrow insecure-code fine-tunes raise coherent harmful compliance on harmful-request benchmarks across model families, often beyond the fine-tuned model.

fits_no_version.finding: Insecure-code LoRA FT raised harmful-request MAP in the Qwen models (e.g. 0%→19.81% / 28.67% for Qwen3.5-27B). It did not in Gemma3-12B StrongREJECT (2.88%→1.92%) or Llama3.1-8B StrongREJECT (2.24%→0.64%). Secure-code FT also raised it (9.90% / 15.00%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow code fine-tuning, including on secure code, can erode refusal of harmful requests, with insecure code eroding it more in Qwen3.5-27B. This is a harmful-compliance effect, not the neutral-question EM measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Secure-code-derived steering gave 0.00% MAP on both benchmarks, with nearly all responses coherent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering-induced harmful compliance depends on the source fine-tune: secure-code vectors do not induce it.

fits_no_version.finding: Vectors from bad medical, risky financial and extreme-sports fine-tunes raised MAP above base on both benchmarks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering vectors from several narrow misaligned-data fine-tunes raise harmful-request compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: MAP is non-monotonic in α: it peaks at 2.5 (37.38%) and falls to 0% at α=5, with coherence collapsing to 4/313 passing. It is also strongly layer-dependent: 33.55% at layers 22–25 vs 0.32% at 24–25.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering-induced harmful compliance is sensitive to strength and layer, and high-strength drops reflect degeneration rather than safety.

record.problems: The reported benchmarks consist of harmful requests rather than neutral open-ended questions. Main comparisons use generation seed 0; no uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported. MAP combines harmfulness and coherence, so output degeneration can reduce the measure without indicating safe behavior. The one- versus three-epoch comparison does not isolate epoch count because learning rates and some other settings also vary.
record.rows_left_out: The low-rank projection sweep (Table 7, k = 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15), fine-tuning-configuration comparison (Figure 5(c), Table 8), 21-window layer exploration, detailed per-category benchmark plots (Figures 3 and 10–14), and further example outputs were not transcribed into rows. These are activation-steering results outside the listed versions; the paper describes the projection trend as increasing and saturating at k = 10, and reports that three-epoch configurations yield higher MAP than one-epoch configurations while noting confounds.

untested.parts: Misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions after insecure-code FT; matched controls on that measure. Only harmful-request compliance is measured.
Whether medical, financial or extreme-sports fine-tunes themselves produce broad misalignment; only steering vectors from them are evaluated.
No test of a shared direction across fine-tunes. Each dataset yields its own vector, and the low-rank sweep is within one vector.
No seed variation, no training-trajectory analysis of FT-induced EM on the claim's measure. Model-size results concern steering MAP on harmful requests.

record.verdict_notes: Gemma3-12B and Llama3.1-8B FT values on StrongREJECT fell below base, so 'FT increases MAP' holds only for some models. All main results use a single generation seed with no uncertainty reported. Same-config MAP differs between Table 1 (23.32%) and Table 7 (33.55%). The epoch comparison is confounded by learning-rate and LoRA changes. Base Qwen3.5 checkpoints are listed without '-Instruct', but the paper treats them as aligned (all StrongREJECT responses judged refusals).

versions.untested_parts: The reported behavior measures compliance with harmful instructions, not misaligned free-form answers to neutral questions; the secure-code condition is a control for steering vectors, not a matched benign fine-tuning result on the claimed behavior.

Bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports fine-tunes are used to construct steering vectors; the paper does not test whether the fine-tuned models themselves show the claimed misalignment on neutral prompts.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is evaluated.
The paper does not test whether a shared linear direction or persona feature mediates the behavior across fine-tunes.
No inoculation framing or benign retraining mitigation is evaluated.

The paper studies model scale and coherence-filtered MAP for activation steering, not the size, seed robustness, coherence-filter robustness, or training-stage behavior of the claimed fine-tuning effect.
